The authors have presented a case of a female child who presented with extensive burns on admission causing death within 7 days. The autopsy revealed death due to complications of scald injuries. Also puts forth the details of police inquest and lack of emergent care provided at a rural location and delay in treatment in the burn center. Unfortunately, the manner of death was not determined due to reasons provided in the case. The authors also provide the major issue of lack of awareness leading to such preventable causes of injury.

The authors did provide the images, however, the details on the child's presentation on arrival, complications of burns, and seven days treatment in hospital are not discussed in detail.  Maybe considering adding a few more details on how to differentiate child abuse in immersion burns from accidental burns in forensic practice will be helpful for readers in the discussion part of the paper.

The paper entitled »Computerised eye-tracking as a tool for early cognitive assessment in the preverbal child« describes the methodology for eye-tracking studies with preverbal children. It provides a standardized laboratory setup, calibration, and data preprocessing protocol. Such standardization should allow for greater reproducibility and comparability of studies.

Overall, the paper is understandable, and I find it useful, but I have several comments that might further increase its clarity (page numbers refer to the pdf version of the article):

p. 3, paragraph 5: Fiedler et al. (preprint, 2020) - This source can probably be updated. The last sentence in this paragraph is unclear (please check the use of semicolons).

p. 4, paragraph 6: The last ET measure, i.e., smooth pursuit, is not described clearly. What exactly is used as a measure here?

p. 5, paragraph 1: To make the percentage number of fixations clearer, it would be better to write »the percentage number of fixations within a selected area of interest« instead.

The numbering of references is incorrect from this page on (e.g., Reference 38 should be 39, and subsequent references should be renumbered).

p. 8, paragraph 3: A description of the moving stimulus used for calibration would be helpful. How much did the stimulus move? How might this affect the accuracy (and precision) of the calibration?

p. 10, paragraph 1: The description of the validity codes used by Tobii is unclear. The authors write that the lower the value, the more certain the eye tracker found the eye. Then they write that they discarded the validity codes that are less than or equal to 2. In this paragraph, it would also be helpful to describe in more detail the criterion by which the outliers were removed.

p. 10, paragraph 2: In this paragraph, the authors list the data collected. Later, they do not report this data.

p. 11, Table 1: Perhaps the authors could delete this table. The reader cannot understand the data in this table because the tasks the children were asked to perform (working memory, visual attention, social cognition tasks) are not described in detail in the text. It is unclear what the measures presented in Table 1 refer to (e.g., what are baseline, gap, and overlap?). Why are the results of the social cognition task not shown as well? In my opinion, only the first row of the table is relevant to the present content of the paper (it indirectly indicates the compliance of the participating children and how successfully data were collected from them).

Perhaps instead of the information shown in Table 1, the authors could show the validity of the calibration for all participants and some of the ET data they collected (mentioned in paragraph 2 of p. 10). They might also describe and discuss their difficulties in trying to derive/calculate the listed ET measures (if any).

In the Extended Data file, the authors present an inventory of children's behaviors (last table). It is unclear what the purpose of this inventory was, how it was used in the present study, and whether this inventory should be a part of the standardized protocol the authors propose and why.

I confirm that I have read this submission and believe that I have an appropriate level of expertise to state that I do not consider it to be of an acceptable scientific standard, for reasons outlined above.

The genomic and clinical features of the COVID-19 Omicron variant: a narrative review. (Hertanto 
                et al.)

Summary:

The ongoing COVID-19 pandemic is a major cause of worldwide mortality and morbidity. The review manuscript by Hertanto 
                et al. looks at the Omicron variant that first emerged in South Africa in November of 2021 and how it became a Variant of Concern relatively quickly. This review paper is split into two parts, the first covers the genomic basis of the Omicron variant and the second part looks at the clinical features of the same variant.

Major comments:

What we find lacking in this review is that authors fail to introduce the readers to any basic background of Omicron. There are phylogenetic studies that point to the suggestion that the Omicron variant likely diverged early on from other SARS-CoV-2 strains. Examination of the whole genome has indicated that the Omicron variant can be classified into two different lineages, BA.1 and BA.2. Maybe more could have been presented on this earlier rather than at the end in the highlights section of the paper. If this is a narrative review, the hope is that an overall picture of the subject is presented. We find that this is lacking in this narrative.

The major focus of the section on the genomic bases of the Omicron variant is on the mutations that are present in the 3 key regions of the spike of SARS-CoV-2: the receptor binding domain, the N-terminal domain and the furin cleavage site. There are more than just the mutations found in these three regions that account for the mutations present in the Omicron variant. The authors do not cover these mutations or their effect.

The first sentence in Mutations in RBD section: "As displayed in Table 2, the N501Y mutation that converts amino acid asparagine to tyrosine at position 501 was identified in the Omicron variant", is slightly misleading. On first read, it implies that this mutation was identified first in the Omicron variant. This mutation has been identified in other variants, and this is represented five sentences later in the same paragraph.

On the section titled: What can we tell from the Ct value of patients with the Omicron variant? : While the authors present that Omicron variant samples had a higher Ct value compared to other variant samples, there is nothing notable to take away from this section. The authors do not highlight any key point as to what having a higher Ct value means for the Omicron variant.

Minor Comments:

Table 2: Reported mutations in S-protein of the Omicron variant. This table was not helpful and did not contribute anything to the review. All the mutations identified in the Omicron variant should have been presented, not just the ones in the RBD, NTD and Furin Cleavage site. Legend for Table 2 mentions the mutations that are potentially suitable for Omicron screening but no where in the body of the text is there mention of using the mutations for screening purposes.

Clinical features of the Omicron variant:

For this section of the paper, the authors highlight the different clinical patterns observed in the Omicron variant compared to its predecessors. This section is written and presented very well. Being able to read some comparisons between the Omicron, Alpha and Delta variant was a plus and helped accomplish the author’s goal. With the presentation of the Omicron came asymptomatic and symptomatic variant infection. It would be a nice touch if the authors mentioned something notable about this occurrence.

The data presented in Table 3 might have been better served if presented in graph/chart form. It would have had a better impact if that data was presented differently.

Summary:

Overall, this review is missing in many areas. There is no new scientific information that is presented. There are other reviews, (1: Omicron genetic and clinical peculiarities that may overturn SARS-CoV-2 pandemic: a literature review; 2: Literature review of Omicron: A grim reality amidst COVID-19) that give a good understanding of the Omicron variant and the impact on the COVID-19 pandemic.

This study examines determinants of women's participation in community health insurance, employer provided insurance, and private health insurance. The analysis is based on DHS data from 2016.

My understanding is that Uganda also "introduced health financing reforms that entailed abolition of user fees, and in due process planned to introduce a National Health Insurance Scheme (NHIS)"

This was discussed in the following paper: 
                https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC10125197/

While the descriptive analysis in the current paper is interesting, it is not entirely clear to me how well enrollment in health insurance in 2016 predicts enrollment in 2023. Can the authors explain (based on other papers using different datasets) how much health insurance enrollment in Uganda has increased since 2016? And have people started enrolling in the national health insurance scheme already? If yes, how relevant are these analyses from 2016 for the current situation?

I also see that the enrollment of women is very low in 2016. However, it is unclear to me whether women can possibly make use of the health insurance of other household members? It would be good if the authors could explain this for readers such as myself who are less familiar with these specific details of the health insurance context in Uganda.

I would also be interested in learning more about the specific hypotheses the authors had in mind when they started the analyses. Did they expect higher correlations between access to media and private health insurance because of advertisements? Or did they have other specific hypotheses. Currently, the paper presents lots of correlations, but it is unclear how to interpret those without understanding the conceptual framework the authors had in mind when examining the correlations. Theory seems to be missing from the current version of the paper.

I do also think that it is important to stay away from language using causal connotation considering the cross-sectional nature of the DHS data used by the authors. The authors currently speak about effects, but I do not think that is correct considering that they are merely looking at correlations. The correlations are interesting, but I would highly recommend not interpreting them as causal relationships.

It is also a bit unclear to me why the authors claim that no study "has assessed the effect of demographic and media factors on women’s demand for different types of health insurance among women, with a focus on a developing country (in this case, specifically Uganda)." I just searched on google scholar and found several studies examining this relationship, such as the ones in the links below:

https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/abs/10.1002/hpm.2505

https://journals.plos.org/plosone/article?id=10.1371/journal.pone.0248411

The paper makes a contribution even when it is not the first to examine the relationship and even without establishing causal relationships. I would use much more cautious language when describing the correlations and when describing the contribution of the paper. This is also important to do in the discussion and conclusion when interpreting the results.

I have a few methodological comments as well. First, it is unclear to me why the authors use firth logistic regression. I am not an expert, but my understanding is that firth logistic regression is used when sample sizes are small. That's not the case here. I would instead recommend using a multinominal logistic regression so that the authors can examine all health insurance choices in one model. The paper in the link below does something similar when they examine choices to enroll in the Ghanaian national health insurance scheme:

https:/www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/abs/pii/S0277953610007744

This choice allows the authors to also account for households that initially enroll but then drop out from the national health insurance scheme.

Alternatively, can use a usual logistic regression model, but I think a multinominal regression model accounting for different types of health insurance may be beneficial when analyzing the results.

Further, I am not sure I understand the probability values in Table 2. Do these refer to p-values? If yes, why are they not reported for each relationship? I think this table requires some changes to make the reporting clearer. It would also be beneficial to show percentages in this table as opposed to only absolute numbers. This would make comparisons easier (at least for myself).

Overall, I think the paper has potential but would benefit from some of the suggested changes above when interpreting the results.

The authors address an important problem in patient care. Burnout and exhaustion are downsides in people caring for others, which can lead to enormous personal and occupational problems such as, for example, poor mental health, frequent sick leaves and increased error rates. In extreme cases, permanent sick leaves can lead to shutdown of health services.

My biggest concern is the generalizability of the studies' findings. The authors use self-reports in a voluntary online survey. All members of the relevant association of gastroenterologist in Germany have been invited to take part. It has not been described how this invitation was accomplished (eg on the association's periodical, electronic newsletter, etc.) and whether members have been reminded in case they did not take part. It has not been described if any measures have been implemented to avoid double entries. About a fourth of the invited members took part in the online survey. Although the authors write that "the sample characteristics were compared to membership characteristics of the Federal Association of Gastroenterology in Germany as these members are considered to be a representative sample for the population of gastroenterologists" the reader does not learn which characteristics have been compared and what the results were in detail. Possibly, these findings can be added to the manuscript. Thus, even in case the members of the association are a representative sample of all gastroenterologists in Germany, the reader does not get to know details why the members who responded to the online survey are representative for the association's members. With a view to the relevant outcome of this study, it seems conceivable that only those physicians who are less exhausted by their work took the time for the survey. As a consequence, more severe cases of burnout might be missed in the analysis and the predictive value of the fitted models might be better in mild cases of exhaustion.

The second biggest concern refers to confounding. The findings in the manuscript come from an observational study and by such are prone to possible confounding. As a reader of the study findings, I am interested in what has been done to reduce the effect of possible confounding. Unfortunately, this has not been described in the manuscript. The authors are aware about the limitations of voluntary self-report and state "We collected cross-sectional data based on self-reports which always have to be interpreted with caution", but it would be helpful for the readers if the authors could comment in which way and regarding which aspects the readers should be cautious.

The authors shared the data in a public repository, which is excellent. A description of the variables would be helpful. The relevant reporting guideline (STROBE for cross-sectional studies) has been used. The uploaded data set occasionally contains missing values. In the main text, it has not been described how these have been treated during analysis. As the statistics software usually deletes subjects with missing values, I guess this is the method that has implicitly been used.
